Daniel’s “tpmorp” framing usefully spotlights a real trick in prompt-based classification—turn labels into *continuations* and score them—but it also inherits a quiet, central assumption: that a language model’s raw continuation likelihood is a reliable proxy for the semantic event you care about (“player is poisoned”). In practice, those scores are dominated by nuisances: length (shorter completions win), genericity (“the player becomes ill” may be globally more probable than “the tea becomes angry”), and prompt priors (some phrasings are simply more “LM-natural”). The result is that the method can drift from *relation to A* toward *fluency under the model*. This is why much of the prompt-learning literature ends up adding calibration or normalization—e.g., subtracting a “null” baseline or using likelihood ratios/PMI-style scoring—rather than trusting raw log-probs as-is (see the calibration discussion around prompt-based learning in [Zhao et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.09690)). Without that, an ensemble of tpmorps can become an ensemble of stylistic hacks.

A second blind spot is that Daniel’s “learn weights by gradient descend” step is, functionally, a linear classifier over LM-derived features (log-likelihoods of alternative verbalizations). That is not a criticism—done carefully, it’s a clean way to repurpose a frozen LM—but it changes the narrative: the intelligence is no longer “in the LM alone,” it’s in a supervised layer plus a hand-designed feature map. This is essentially the same lineage as pattern/verbalizer methods like [PET](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.07676): multiple templates/verbalizers, aggregated and trained, often with self-training. The interesting question then becomes comparative: if Daniel already has `(free-input text, outcome)` tuples, when does “tpmorp + learned weights” outperform a straightforward classifier head or lightweight finetuning, and what is the sample-efficiency tradeoff? That’s where the post could sharpen its claim.

Finally, the “automatic tpmorp proposal” loop gestures at interpretability (“humans can inspect the ensembles”), but interpretability here is fragile: the system is incentivized to discover *any* continuation whose probability correlates with labels, including spurious correlates tied to wording artifacts in the dataset. In a dungeon-game setting, the deeper omission is world-state grounding: whether tea can be “angry” is not just a linguistic regularity but a rule of the game. If the scoring mechanism is trained only on text/outcome pairs, it may learn dataset-specific shortcuts rather than a reusable action-to-state transition model; inspecting tpmorps after the fact may reveal *what it latched onto*, but not guarantee it learned the intended causal semantics. This doesn’t make the idea bad—it clarifies that the core difficulty is less “can we find good tpmorps?” and more “can we prevent the tpmorps from becoming an elegant interface to spurious correlation.”
